results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Chest pain, trouble breathing and fainting are emergencies whether you are pregnant or just gave birth. Do not drive yourself. If you are alone, call and stay on the line.
watchFor: Say how many weeks pregnant you are, or how many days since the birth
Unlock the door so they can get in

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: Anything that worries you is worth a call, and the triage line exists for exactly this. Say what changed and when it started. If you cannot reach them and it is getting worse, go to the ER.
watchFor: Pain that gets worse rather than better
A fever on top of it
Bleeding that starts

results.headline: Call your OB triage line and describe it.
results.body: Light spotting with no pain is common in early pregnancy, and it is still worth a call so someone who knows your history can decide. Call today rather than waiting for the next appointment.
watchFor: Bleeding that fills a pad
Cramps or pain with the bleeding
Sharp pain on one side, or pain in the tip of your shoulder

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Bleeding that fills a pad, or bleeding with pain, needs to be looked at today. Call and describe how much and how fast. If you cannot reach them, go to the ER.
watchFor: Filling a pad in an hour
Clots
Dizziness or fainting

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Fluid that keeps leaking can mean the waters have broken, and that needs to be checked today whatever week you are in. Note the colour before you call.

sources.title: How to tell when labor begins

watchFor: Fluid that is green, brown, or smells bad
Contractions starting
A fever

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Movements that are clearly fewer than usual are checked the same day, not at the next appointment. Do not wait to see whether they pick up overnight.

sources.title: Special tests for monitoring fetal well-being

watchFor: No movement at all
A change in the kind of movement, not just the amount
A fever or bleeding on top of it

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now, and go in if you cannot reach them.
results.body: Not feeling the baby move is the one thing on this page that is never waited on. Call, and if the line does not answer, go to the unit.

sources.title: Special tests for monitoring fetal well-being

watchFor: Anything at all that feels different
Bleeding
A headache with vision changes

results.headline: Count again in an hour, and call if the count is low.
results.body: Movements that came back after resting and eating are a good sign, and they are not a reason to stop paying attention. Lie on your left side and count. Fewer than ten movements in two hours is a call.

sources.title: Special tests for monitoring fetal well-being

watchFor: Fewer than ten movements in two hours
Movements that stop again
A change from the baby's usual pattern

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: A severe headache, or seeing spots or flashing lights, can be a sign of preeclampsia, and it is checked the same day. Say that you have a headache and vision changes when you call — those two words get you seen faster.
watchFor: Swelling in your face or hands
Pain under your ribs on the right
Nausea that comes back after the first trimester

results.headline: Call your OB triage line if it gets worse or comes with anything else.
results.body: A headache on its own is common and treatable. What makes it worth a call is severity, or company: vision changes, swelling, or pain under the ribs. Write down when it started.
watchFor: It becomes severe
Spots or flashing lights
Swelling in your face or hands

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in pregnancy is looked at the same day. Say the temperature and how you took it. Do not take anything for it before you call unless you have already been told to.
watchFor: A fever that does not come down
Pain when you pee
Contractions or bleeding

results.headline: Call your OB triage line if it reaches 100.4°F (38°C).
results.body: A low fever is worth watching rather than ignoring. Take it again in a few hours with the same thermometer, and write the number down so you can read it out.
watchFor: It reaches 100.4°F (38°C)
It lasts more than a day
Any other symptom arriving with it

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Preeclampsia can start for the first time after the birth, usually in the first week. A severe headache or changed vision after giving birth is checked the same day, not at the six-week visit.
watchFor: Swelling in your face or hands
Pain under your ribs on the right
A blood pressure you can have checked today

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: A fever over 100.4°F (38°C) in the first weeks after birth needs to be looked at today. It can be an infection that is easy to treat and not easy to wait out.
watchFor: Foul-smelling discharge
Pain or redness in a caesarean incision
Pain in one breast with redness

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Soaking a pad in an hour after giving birth is an emergency. Do not wait to see whether it slows. Call, and have someone stay with the baby.
watchFor: Feeling faint, dizzy, or cold
A racing heart
Clots bigger than a golf ball

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: A clot bigger than a golf ball, or any clot with heavy bleeding, is an emergency. Bleeding that heavy can make you faint quickly, so call before you do anything else.
watchFor: Feeling faint or dizzy
Bleeding that does not slow
A racing heart

results.headline: Call your OB triage line if it gets heavier.
results.body: Bleeding that is lighter than yesterday is the direction it is meant to go. It can come back a little when you do more, and it should not come back heavy.
watchFor: It gets heavier rather than lighter
Clots
A fever, or discharge that smells bad

results.headline: Call or text 988 now.
results.body: Thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby are a medical emergency and they are treatable. 988 is free, answered 24 hours a day, and you do not have to be in crisis to call. If you are in immediate danger, call 911.
watchFor: Call 911 if you or the baby are in immediate danger
Tell one person near you, now
You can call 988 as many times as you need

results.headline: Call the PSI Helpline today.
results.body: Not coping is a reason to call, and it does not have to be the worst day. The PSI Helpline is free, and the people who answer know what the first year is like. 1-800-944-4773.
watchFor: It getting worse rather than better
Not sleeping even when the baby sleeps
Thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby — that is 988 or 911

results.headline: Call the PSI Helpline if this lasts more than two weeks.
results.body: Most people feel raw in the first weeks, and it usually eases. What is worth a call is duration and direction: two weeks, or getting worse. You do not need a reason beyond that.
watchFor: It lasts more than two weeks
It gets worse rather than better
You stop enjoying things you used to

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: Anything that worries you in the first weeks after birth is worth a call. The triage line is there for this, and calling it is not a fuss.
watchFor: A fever
Pain that gets worse
Bleeding that gets heavier

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Fast or laboured breathing, or a blue tint around the lips, is an emergency at any age. Do not drive the baby yourself. Call and stay on the line.
watchFor: Ribs pulling in with each breath
Pauses in breathing
Flaring nostrils or grunting

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A baby who is not feeding, or who has far fewer wet diapers than usual, is seen the same day. Count the wet diapers before you call — the number is the useful part.

sources.title: How often and how much should your baby eat

watchFor: Fewer than six wet diapers in a day after the first week
Refusing feeds for more than a few hours
A dry mouth, or no tears when crying

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: A baby who cannot breathe, cough, or make a sound is choking. Start back blows and chest thrusts if you know them, and have someone call 911 while you do.
watchFor: Call before you start if you are alone and can put the phone on speaker
Do not put your fingers in the mouth unless you can see the object
Keep going until the baby breathes or help arrives

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A baby who is hard to wake, or who is unusually sleepy, is seen the same day. Try to wake them for a feed first, and note whether they wake and whether they feed.

sources.title: How often and how much should your baby eat

watchFor: Not waking for a feed
A temperature under 97.5°F or over 100.4°F
A change in colour or breathing

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now. A fever under 3 months is an ER visit.
results.body: A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby under 3 months is not watched at home. Call, and expect to be sent to be seen today. Take the temperature again on the way.
watchFor: Any fever at all in a baby under 3 months
A temperature under 97.5°F (36.4°C)
Not feeding, or hard to wake

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A fever with unusual sleepiness, a rash, trouble breathing, or refusing feeds is seen the same day. Say all of the symptoms when you call, not just the fever.
watchFor: A rash that does not fade when you press it
Trouble breathing
Not waking for feeds

results.headline: Call your pediatrician if the fever lasts more than three days.
results.body: A fever on its own in an older baby is usually something that passes. What matters is how the baby is between the temperatures, and how long it lasts.
watchFor: More than three days
A rash, or unusual sleepiness
Refusing feeds, or far fewer wet diapers

results.headline: Call your pediatrician if the rash does not fade when you press it.
results.body: Most rashes in a baby who is feeding and alert are not urgent. The one test worth knowing: press a clear glass on it. A rash that stays visible under the glass is a call.
watchFor: A rash that does not fade under pressure
A fever arriving with it
The baby becoming sleepy or refusing feeds

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A rash in a baby who is also sleepy or not feeding is seen the same day. Describe both things when you call.
watchFor: A rash that does not fade under pressure
A fever
Not feeding, or hard to wake

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: Describe what you are seeing, how long it has been going on, and whether your child is drinking and playing. If the office is closed, use the after-hours line. If your child gets worse while you wait, call 911.
watchFor: Breathing that gets faster or harder
A child who stops drinking or stops waking

results.headline: Call Poison Control now: 1-800-222-1222.
results.body: Do not wait for a symptom. Have the container in your hand when you call, and say what it was, how much, and when. Do not make your child vomit. If your child is not breathing or is unconscious, call 911 instead.
watchFor: Keep the container, even if it is empty
Say how much your child weighs

results.headline: Go to the emergency department now.
results.body: A button battery in the throat or nose burns tissue within two hours, and two magnets can pull loops of bowel together. Do not wait for a symptom and do not try to make your child vomit. Call 911 if they are struggling to breathe.
watchFor: Bring the device the battery came from
Do not give food or drink on the way

results.headline: Call Poison Control today: 1-800-222-1222.
results.body: A child who seems well after swallowing something can still need a check. Poison Control will say whether to watch at home or go in, and they answer around the clock. Have the container and your child's weight ready.
watchFor: Vomiting, drooling, or a sudden change in behaviour
A child who gets sleepy or floppy

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: If your child cannot breathe, cough, or make a sound, start back blows and abdominal thrusts for their age and have someone call 911. If they can cough, stay with them and let the cough work. Do not put your fingers in their mouth.
watchFor: Say your child's age and whether they are conscious
Unlock the door so they can get in

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Ribs pulling in, nostrils flaring, grunting, or lips and face turning blue are signs of real trouble. Sit your child up, stay with them, and call. Do not drive yourself if you are alone with a child working this hard to breathe.
watchFor: Say how long they have been like this
Unlock the door so they can get in

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A child who is talking, drinking, and playing between coughs is in a different place from one who is not. Call and describe the sound, when it started, and whether there is a fever. If the work of breathing increases, call 911.
watchFor: Ribs pulling in with each breath
A child who stops drinking or stops talking

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Being knocked out, vomiting more than once, a seizure, clear fluid from the nose or ear, or a child who is not themselves after a bang to the head all need to be seen now. Keep them still and do not let them eat or drink.
watchFor: Say whether they were knocked out and for how long
Do not let them sleep it off on the way

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: A child who cried, then went back to playing, is the usual story after a bump. Call the office the same day so they can decide whether to see them. Wake them once in the night and check they respond as they normally do.
watchFor: Vomiting more than once
Unusual sleepiness, or a headache that gets worse
A pupil that is bigger than the other

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: A stiff neck, light hurting the eyes, a rash that does not fade when you press it, or a child who is very hard to wake all need to be seen immediately. Do not wait for the office to open.
watchFor: Say how high the fever is and how long it has lasted
Unlock the door so they can get in

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: A fever with unusual sleepiness, a rash, trouble breathing, or a child who will not drink is seen the same day. Say all of the symptoms when you call, not just the fever.
watchFor: A rash that does not fade when you press it
Trouble breathing
Not drinking, or hard to wake

results.headline: Call your pediatrician if the fever lasts more than three days.
results.body: A fever on its own in a child who is drinking and playing is usually something that passes. What matters is how they are between the temperatures, and how long it lasts. Offer fluids often.
watchFor: More than three days
A rash, or unusual sleepiness
Not drinking, or far fewer wet diapers

results.headline: Call 911 or go to the emergency department now.
results.body: A burn bigger than your child's palm, or one on the face, hands, feet, or genitals, needs to be seen. Cool it under cool running water for twenty minutes and cover it loosely. Do not put ice, butter, or a cream on it.
watchFor: Keep cooling under running water on the way
Do not break any blisters

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: A small burn with unbroken skin can usually be cared for at home, but the office should hear about it the same day. Cool it under cool running water for twenty minutes, then cover it loosely. Do not put ice on it.
watchFor: A burn that looks deeper, or turns white or charred
Redness that spreads past the burn

results.headline: Call your pediatrician if the rash does not fade when you press it.
results.body: The one test worth knowing: press a clear glass on the rash. A rash that stays visible under the glass is a call. A rash that fades is watched at home, and the office should hear about it if it lasts more than a few days.
watchFor: A rash that does not fade under pressure
A fever arriving with it
A child who becomes sleepy or stops drinking

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: A rash that stays visible when you press a clear glass against it can be a sign of a serious infection. It needs to be seen immediately, especially with a fever. Do not wait to see whether it fades on its own.
watchFor: Say whether there is a fever and how long it has lasted
Unlock the door so they can get in

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Swelling of the lips, tongue, or face, a tight throat, or trouble swallowing after a food, a sting, or a new medicine is an emergency. Use an epinephrine auto-injector if you have one, then call. Say that you gave it.
watchFor: Say what they ate or touched, and when
Say whether you used an auto-injector

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: Redness that is spreading, a bite that is hot and getting bigger, or a sore with pus needs to be looked at. Draw a line around the edge of the redness with a pen so the office can see how fast it is moving.
watchFor: Redness that crosses the line you drew
A fever, or a child who stops drinking

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Contractions that come regularly, a heavy pressure low down, or a low backache that comes and goes can be preterm labor. Call and describe how often they come and how long they last. Do not wait to see whether they stop.
watchFor: Time the contractions before you call
Say how many weeks pregnant you are

sources.title: How to tell when labor begins

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Pain in the belly, and especially pain on one side, needs to be talked through with someone who can see you. Call and describe where it is, when it started, and whether there is bleeding or a fever.
watchFor: Pain that gets worse rather than better
Bleeding, a fever, or feeling faint

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: Not keeping food or water down for a day, losing weight, or feeling dizzy when you stand can lead to dehydration. Call and say how long it has been and how much you are keeping down. There are treatments that help.
watchFor: Not peeing, or dark urine
Feeling faint when you stand up

sources.title: Morning sickness: nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: Burning when you pee, going often, or pain low in the belly can be a urinary tract infection, and those are treated in pregnancy rather than waited out. Call and ask to leave a urine sample.
watchFor: A fever, or pain in your back or side
Blood in your urine

results.headline: Call your OB or your pediatrician today.
results.body: A red, painful, hot patch on one breast, with a fever or flu-like aching, needs to be looked at. Keep feeding or pumping on that side. Call and say when it started and whether you have a fever.
watchFor: A fever that climbs, or a lump that gets bigger
Feeling faint or very unwell

results.headline: Call your OB triage line today.
results.body: A c-section scar or stitches that are red, hot, opening, or leaking pus need to be seen. Call and describe what it looks like. A small amount of clear or pink fluid is common in the first days; pus and spreading redness are not.
watchFor: The wound opening, or pus coming from it
A fever, or redness that spreads

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: One leg that is swollen, hot, or painful, especially in the calf, needs to be checked the same day. Blood clots are more common after birth. Call and say which leg and when you noticed it.
watchFor: Chest pain or sudden breathlessness
Swelling that gets worse through the day

results.headline: Call your OB triage line now.
results.body: Not being able to pee in the first day or two after birth, or a burning that comes with it, needs to be sorted out rather than waited on. Call and say when you last went and whether it hurts.
watchFor: A full, painful bladder you cannot empty
A fever, or blood in your urine

results.headline: Mention it at the next visit.
results.body: Spitting up after feeds is common in the first months. Keep them upright for twenty minutes after a feed, and mention it at the next visit. Call sooner if the spit-up is green or forceful, or if the wet diapers drop.
watchFor: Spit-up that is green or yellow-green
Spit-up that shoots across the room
Fewer wet diapers, or no weight gain

sources.title: How often and how much should your baby eat

results.headline: Go to the emergency department now.
results.body: Green or yellow-green vomit in a baby can mean a blockage in the bowel, and it needs to be seen immediately. Do not feed them on the way. Call 911 if they are hard to wake or struggling to breathe.
watchFor: Bring the last diaper, or a photo of it
Do not feed them on the way

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: Vomiting that shoots across the room, rather than spilling out, is different from spit-up and needs to be looked at. Call and say how often it happens and whether the baby is hungry again straight after.
watchFor: Fewer wet diapers
A baby who is hungry but cannot keep anything down

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: Vomiting more than a few times, or a baby who is keeping nothing down, needs a call the same day. Offer small feeds often. Watch the wet diapers, because that is the clearest sign of whether they are getting enough fluid.
watchFor: No wet diaper for six hours or more
A sunken soft spot, or no tears when crying

sources.title: How often and how much should your baby eat

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: A cord stump that is red at the base, smells bad, or is bleeding needs to be looked at. Keep it dry and let it fall off on its own. Call and describe what you are seeing.
watchFor: Redness spreading onto the skin around the stump
A fever, or a baby who feeds less

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: Crying that will not stop, and a baby who cannot be settled by feeding, a change, or being held, is worth a call. It is also worth putting the baby down safely and stepping away for a few minutes if you feel close to the edge.
watchFor: A cry that sounds different, or is weaker
A baby who stops feeding or stops waking

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: Describe what you are seeing, how long it has been going on, and whether the baby is feeding and having wet diapers. If the office is closed, use the after-hours line. If the baby gets worse while you wait, call 911.
watchFor: Breathing that gets faster or harder
A baby who stops feeding or stops waking

results.headline: Call 911 now.
results.body: Being knocked out, vomiting more than once, a seizure, or a baby who is not themselves after a bang to the head needs to be seen now. Keep them still and do not feed them on the way.
watchFor: Say whether they were knocked out and for how long
Do not feed them on the way

results.headline: Call your pediatrician today.
results.body: A baby who cried, then fed and settled, is the usual story after a small bump. Call the office the same day so they can decide whether to see them. Wake them once in the night and check they feed as they normally do.
watchFor: Vomiting more than once
Unusual sleepiness, or a soft spot that bulges
A pupil that is bigger than the other

results.headline: Call your pediatrician now.
results.body: Yellow skin or eyes in the first 24 hours, or yellow that is spreading to the belly or legs, needs to be checked the same day. Call and say how old the baby is and where the yellow reaches.
watchFor: Yellow in the first 24 hours of life
A baby who is sleepier than usual or feeding less

results.headline: Mention it at the next visit.
results.body: Yellow that shows up after the first day and stays on the face is the usual pattern. Feed often, because feeding is what clears it, and mention it at the next visit. Call sooner if the yellow spreads or the baby is sleepier.
watchFor: Yellow spreading to the belly, arms, or legs
A baby who is hard to wake for feeds
